newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australia dlr relieved by reversal in Japan yields.
newsitem.headline: Australia dlr relieved by reversal in Japan yields.

text.p: A sudden setback for the yen helped the Australian dollar shrug off early softness Thursday, although the currency again failed to clear key resistance.

The dollar was pinned at US$0.7635 support for much of the day but won a reprieve when Japanese industrial production data proved far weaker than expected. The shock 0.4 percent fall in output forced the market to reconsider its assumption BOJ rates would be rising soon and JGB bond yields turned sharply lower.
The local currency leapt a yen in response, which helped it steady elsewhere, but dealers emphasised it still needed to clear US$0.7675 at the minimum to counter the bearish trend.
By 5.00 pm (0700 GMT) the dollar was girding its loins at US$0.7652/57 after meeting heavy offers at US$0.7670 and was barely moved on Wednesday's late US$0.7651/56.

It did dip as deep at US$0.7615 overnight as U.S. and local banks sought to trigger big stop loss sales, only to bounce as high as US$0.7665 as corporate demand forced a round of distressed short covering.

Chart watchers reckoned there was still room for a squeeze to US$0.7720, so partly filling the gap left by Friday's dive from US$0.7770. But even bulls thought this would be a prelude to further weakness and as test of the 1997 lowe at US$0.7550.

On the crosses the currency had lost ground to the yen as Japanese bond rates continued heavenward, but bounced back when the industrial output data showed a surprise 0.4 percent fall, taking annual growth to 4.9 percent from 7.6 percent.

The key 10-year JGB contract had dived to 2.630 percent by the local close after earlier climbing to a year high of 2.750 percent in the belief a strong production figure would hasten a hike by the Bank of Japan.
The dollar rallied to 89.20/30 yen by the finish from an 88.11 low and was even a notch up on Wednesday's 88.70/80 close. It also firmed to 58.4 in trade weighted terms from 58.3.
On the domestic front inventory data proved unexpectedly weak and promised to depress GDP growth in the first quarter.
Business stocks fell 2.1 percent, the first drop since the September quarter of 1993, and forced analysts to hastily revise down forecasts for Q1 GDP growth to below 1.0 percent.
That meant annual growth was set to slow sharply from the 3.1 percent seen in Q4 -- even 1.0 percent would see a retreat to 2.4 percent on the year.
However, the rundown in stocks confirmed retail sales had been robust in the quarter and suggested industrial production would pick up in Q2/Q3 as inventory levels were re-built.
This natural pick-up could be expected to be supported by last week's policy easing thus raising the chance that growth might surprise on the upside in 1997/98.

Today's other data showed Australian exports performed strongly in April to swing the balance of international goods and services to a surplus of A$300 million from a deficit of A$103 million in March.

Goods exports rose eight percent while imports were flat on the month. The data suggested the country's current account deficit was still some way from becoming a burden again and should support dollar sentiment at the margin.
More interesting will be quarterly balance of payments data for Q1 on Friday since they will contain the first estimate of the current account deficit now that monthly figures have been dropped.

Also out Friday are April retail trade and motor vehicle registrations and both will be scrutinsed more closely than usual for the slightest hint about where RBA policy is heading next. Sales are expected to rise 0.5 percent after a soft 0.3 percent fall in March, while registrations are seen flat after a 1.3 percent gain the month before.
